claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 has a disordered BCC state at high temperature.
The stability of the initial BCC phase is governed by competition between configurational-entropy stabilization and an Al-induced thermodynamic driving force for local chemical ordering.
At elevated temperature, configurational entropy stabilizes a random, homogeneous BCC solid solution in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Cooling reduces the entropy contribution that stabilizes the homogeneous phase.
Al has chemical affinities in this alloy that promote local ordering during cooling or annealing.
Al-centered local ordering produces short-range clustering of other constituent elements.
Al-induced local ordering lowers the local free energy sufficiently to destabilize BCC and trigger a phase transformation.
Slow cooling can promote compositional segregation or secondary-phase precipitation in a multicomponent Cr-containing alloy.
Rapid quenching kinetically retains the high-temperature disordered BCC structure in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples will remain homogeneous and BCC.
Slowly cooled or annealed Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples will exhibit more local chemical ordering than rapidly quenched samples.
Slowly cooled or annealed Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples will exhibit composition fluctuations or incipient secondary phases.
A temperature window exists in this alloy in which entropy stabilization and the ordering driving force are competitive.
At temperatures substantially above that window, entropy dominates phase stability.
At much lower temperatures, kinetic limitations may prevent Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 from completing equilibrium phase transformations.
Holding composition and initial state constant while varying cooling or annealing history provides a controlled comparison of the proposed thermal-history effect.

Absence of a statistically significant ordering or phase-separation difference between annealed or slowly cooled samples and the quenched baseline would falsify the proposed governing role of Al-induced ordering.
